cards.front: What do angles on a straight line add to?

options.explanation: A straight line forms a half-turn, which is 180°. Therefore, adjacent angles lying on the same straight line must have a total of 180°.
This confuses a straight line with a full turn around a point. A straight line is a half-turn, so its angles add to 180°.
This mistakes a straight angle for a right angle. A right angle is 90°, but angles on a straight line add to 180°.
This represents three-quarters of a full turn rather than a straight line. A straight line forms a half-turn, so its angles total 180°.

cards.front: Angles around a point add to [ ___ ].
cards.back: Angles around a point add to 360°.

options.explanation: Angles around a single point make one complete turn. A complete turn measures 360°, so all the angles around the point must total 360°.
This confuses angles around a point with angles on a straight line. Around a point is a complete turn, so the angles add to 360°.
This gives the size of one right angle, only a quarter-turn. Angles all the way around a point form a full turn of 360°.
This accounts for only three-quarters of a turn. Angles around a point complete the entire turn, so their total is 360°.

cards.front: What do angles in a triangle add to?

options.explanation: The three interior angles of every triangle have a total of 180°, regardless of the triangle’s side lengths, angle sizes or orientation.
This confuses the triangle’s interior angle sum with a full turn. The three interior angles of any triangle always add to 180°.
A right triangle contains one 90° angle, but that is not the total. All three interior angles of a triangle add to 180°.
This is three right angles, not the interior angle sum of a triangle. Every triangle’s three interior angles have a total of 180°.

cards.front: In a regular polygon, all sides are [ ___ ] and all interior angles are [ ___ ].
cards.back: In a regular polygon, all sides are equal and all interior angles are equal.

options.text: In a regular polygon, all sides are equal and all interior angles are equal.
options.explanation: A polygon is regular only when it is both equilateral and equiangular. Therefore, every side has equal length and every interior angle has equal size.

options.text: In a regular polygon, all sides are parallel and all interior angles are equal.
options.explanation: Regular polygons have equal side lengths, not all parallel sides; adjacent sides must meet. Their interior angles are also equal, so both equality conditions are required.

options.text: In a regular polygon, all sides are equal and all interior angles are different.
options.explanation: Equal sides alone do not give the full definition of a regular polygon. A regular polygon must also have equal interior angles, rather than different ones.

options.text: In a regular polygon, all sides are different and all interior angles are different.
options.explanation: This reverses both defining properties of a regular polygon. For a polygon to be regular, all its sides and all its interior angles must be equal.

cards.front: How many triangles can an n-sided polygon be split into from one vertex?

options.explanation: Drawing diagonals from one vertex divides an n-sided polygon into n - 2 non-overlapping triangles. This result is used to derive the polygon interior angle sum.
This common off-by-one error counts one extra region. Splitting from one vertex creates n - 2 triangles because the chosen vertex belongs to the two boundary sides.
This incorrectly assumes one triangle for every side. Diagonals drawn from one vertex actually divide an n-sided polygon into n - 2 triangles.
This is the number of diagonals drawn from one vertex, not the number of triangles formed. Those diagonals create n - 2 triangles.

cards.front: For an n-sided polygon, the interior angle sum is [ ___ ].
cards.back: For an n-sided polygon, the interior angle sum is (n - 2) × 180°.

options.explanation: An n-sided polygon can be divided from one vertex into n - 2 triangles. Each triangle contributes 180°, giving an interior angle sum of (n - 2) × 180°.
This counts one too many triangles in the polygon. The correct split produces n - 2 triangles, so the interior angle sum is (n - 2) × 180°.
This incorrectly assigns a whole triangle to every side. An n-sided polygon splits into n - 2 triangles, making the sum (n - 2) × 180°.
This uses 360° for each triangle, confusing a triangle’s angle sum with a full turn. Each triangle contributes 180°, so the formula is (n - 2) × 180°.

cards.front: What is the interior angle sum of a pentagon?

options.explanation: A pentagon has five sides, so its interior angle sum is (5 - 2) × 180° = 3 × 180° = 540°.
This effectively uses only two triangles instead of three. A pentagon splits into 5 - 2 = 3 triangles, so its interior angles total 540°.
This is the interior angle sum of a hexagon, not a pentagon. For a pentagon, (5 - 2) × 180° gives 540°.
This multiplies the five sides directly by 180° instead of subtracting two first. The correct calculation is (5 - 2) × 180° = 540°.

cards.front: What is the interior angle sum of a hexagon?

options.explanation: A hexagon has six sides, so its interior angle sum is (6 - 2) × 180° = 4 × 180° = 720°.
This is the interior angle sum of a pentagon and uses only three triangles. A hexagon splits into four triangles, giving a total of 720°.
This uses five triangles, as for a seven-sided polygon. A hexagon forms 6 - 2 = 4 triangles, so its interior angle sum is 720°.
This multiplies the six sides directly by 180° instead of subtracting two. The correct calculation is (6 - 2) × 180° = 720°.

cards.front: A pentagon has angles 98°, 121°, 116°, 85° and x. Find x.

options.explanation: A pentagon’s interior angles total 540°. The four known angles total 420°, so the missing angle is $540° - 420° = 120°$.
This results from using 530° as the pentagon’s angle sum. The correct sum is $(5 - 2) \times 180° = 540°$, giving $540° - 420° = 120°$.
This comes from incorrectly using 550° for the total interior angle sum. A pentagon’s angles total 540°, so the missing angle is $540° - 420° = 120°$.
This commonly follows from adding the four given angles as 400° rather than 420°. Their correct total is 420°, leaving $540° - 420° = 120°$.

cards.front: The exterior angles of a polygon, taking one at each vertex, add to [ ___ ].
cards.back: The exterior angles of a polygon, taking one at each vertex, add to 360°.

options.explanation: One exterior angle at each vertex represents the complete turn made when travelling around the polygon, so the exterior angles always add to 360°.
180° is a half-turn and is also the sum of the angles on a straight line. A complete turn around any polygon is 360°.
90° is a quarter-turn and may be one exterior angle of a square, but all the exterior angles of any polygon add to 360°.
540° is the sum of the interior angles of a pentagon, not the universal exterior-angle sum. One exterior angle per vertex always totals 360°.

cards.front: For a regular polygon with n sides, what is each exterior angle?

options.explanation: The exterior angles of every polygon total 360°. In a regular polygon they are equal, so dividing 360° by the number of sides gives each exterior angle.
This incorrectly uses a half-turn as the exterior-angle total. The exterior angles sum to 360°, so each exterior angle of a regular polygon is $360° \div n$.
Multiplying would make each exterior angle increase as the number of sides increases. The fixed total of 360° must instead be divided equally among $n$ vertices.
The expression $n - 2$ belongs to the formula for the interior-angle sum. Exterior angles total 360°, so each one is $360° \div n$.

cards.front: What is the exterior angle of a regular nonagon?

options.explanation: A nonagon has nine sides. Its equal exterior angles divide the full 360° turn into nine parts, so each measures $360° \div 9 = 40°$.
This incorrectly divides 180° by nine, using a half-turn rather than the full exterior-angle total. The correct calculation is $360° \div 9 = 40°$.
45° is the exterior angle of a regular octagon, which has eight sides. A nonagon has nine sides, so its exterior angle is $360° \div 9 = 40°$.
This does not divide the complete 360° turn equally among nine vertices. For a regular nonagon, each exterior angle is $360° \div 9 = 40°$.

cards.front: At each corner, the interior angle and adjacent exterior angle add to [ ___ ].
cards.back: At each corner, the interior angle and adjacent exterior angle add to 180°.

options.explanation: An interior angle and its adjacent exterior angle lie on a straight line. Angles on a straight line are supplementary, so they add to 180°.
360° is the total of one exterior angle at every vertex, not the pair at one corner. An adjacent interior and exterior angle form a straight line totalling 180°.
90° is a right angle, but the adjacent interior and exterior angles form a straight line rather than a right angle. Their sum is therefore 180°.
270° is a three-quarter turn and does not describe this linear pair. Adjacent interior and exterior angles lie on a straight line, so their sum is 180°.

cards.front: A regular 12-sided polygon has exterior angle 30°. What is its interior angle?

options.explanation: The interior angle and adjacent exterior angle add to 180°. Therefore, the interior angle is $180° - 30° = 150°$.
This repeats the exterior angle instead of finding its supplement. The adjacent interior and exterior angles total 180°, so the interior angle is $180° - 30° = 150°$.
This may come from subtracting 30° twice from 180°. Only one adjacent exterior angle is subtracted, giving an interior angle of $180° - 30° = 150°$.
This subtracts the exterior angle from a full turn, but the interior angle forms a straight line with it. The correct calculation is $180° - 30° = 150°$.

cards.front: How do you find the number of sides from a regular polygon's exterior angle?

options.explanation: The equal exterior angles total 360°. Dividing that total by the size of one exterior angle gives how many equal angles, and therefore how many sides, the polygon has.
This uses 180°, the angle on a straight line, instead of the complete exterior-angle total. The number of sides is $360° \div$ the exterior angle.
Multiplication does not determine how many equal exterior angles fit into 360°. The correct operation is division: $n = 360° \div \text{exterior angle}$.
This reverses the division and would give a value below one for ordinary exterior angles. Divide the full 360° turn by one exterior angle to find $n$.

cards.front: A regular polygon has exterior angle 30°. How many sides does it have?

options.explanation: The exterior angles total 360°, and each is 30°. Therefore, the number of equal angles and sides is $360° \div 30° = 12$.
This comes from dividing 180° by 30°, using a half-turn instead of the full exterior-angle total. The correct calculation is $360° \div 30° = 12$ sides.
Ten sides would give each exterior angle as $360° \div 10 = 36°$, not 30°. An exterior angle of 30° gives $360° \div 30° = 12$ sides.
Fifteen sides would produce an exterior angle of $360° \div 15 = 24°$. For an exterior angle of 30°, the polygon has $360° \div 30° = 12$ sides.

cards.front: If given a regular polygon's interior angle, first find the exterior angle using [ ___ ].
cards.back: If given a regular polygon's interior angle, first find the exterior angle using 180° - interior angle.

options.explanation: An interior angle and its corresponding exterior angle lie on a straight line, so they total 180°. Therefore, subtract the interior angle from 180°.
Using 360° confuses angles around a point with supplementary interior and exterior angles. The correct calculation is 180° - interior angle because the two form a straight line.
Adding the angles ignores that their total must be 180°. The exterior angle is found using 180° - interior angle because adjacent interior and exterior angles are supplementary.
Reversing the subtraction produces a negative value for an ordinary convex polygon. The correct exterior angle is 180° - interior angle, giving a positive angle.

cards.front: A regular polygon has interior angle 156°. How many sides does it have?

options.explanation: The exterior angle is 180° - 156° = 24°. Since regular exterior angles total 360°, the polygon has 360° ÷ 24° = 15 sides.
This mistakes the 24° exterior angle for the number of sides. Dividing 360° by 24° gives the correct number, which is 15 sides.
This is an off-by-one error. The exterior angle is 24°, and 360° ÷ 24° equals exactly 15, so the polygon has 15 sides.
This does not follow from the exterior-angle calculation. The exterior angle is 180° - 156° = 24°, so 360° ÷ 24° gives 15 sides.

cards.front: Why must you not divide the interior angle sum by the number of sides for an irregular polygon?
cards.back: Its angles are not all equal.

options.text: Its angles are not all equal.
options.explanation: Dividing the angle sum by the number of sides gives only the mean angle. In an irregular polygon, the individual interior angles are not necessarily equal to that mean.
Equal interior angles would make division useful for finding each angle, as in a regular polygon. An irregular polygon’s angles are not all equal, so division gives only an average.

options.text: Its sides are not all equal.
options.explanation: Unequal side lengths do not directly prevent calculating individual angles from the sum. The relevant issue is that an irregular polygon’s interior angles are not all equal.

options.text: Its angle sum is not fixed.
options.explanation: The interior angle sum is fixed by the number of sides, even for an irregular polygon. Division fails because its individual angles are not all equal.

cards.front: Two missing angles are y and 2y and add to 210°. Find y.

options.explanation: The two angles give y + 2y = 210°, so 3y = 210°. Dividing both sides by 3 gives y = 70°.
This comes from dividing 210° by 2, but the coefficients total 3 because y + 2y = 3y. Dividing by 3 gives y = 70°.
This treats 2y as the required value rather than y. Solving y + 2y = 210° gives y = 70°, while 2y equals 140°.
This uses the total of both missing angles as the value of y. Since y + 2y = 3y, the total must be divided by 3, giving 70°.

cards.front: When polygons meet at a point, which angles usually make the 360° total?

options.explanation: At a shared vertex, the polygons’ interior angles fit together around the point. Angles around a point total 360°, so these are the angles normally added.
The angles filling the space around the shared point are normally the polygons’ interior angles. Exterior angles lie outside each polygon and are not the angles being combined here.
Central angles are measured at a polygon’s centre, not at a vertex where polygons meet. The interior angles at the shared vertex make the 360° total.
Reflex angles are greater than 180° and are not normally the polygon angles fitted around a shared vertex. The relevant angles are the interior angles touching the point.

cards.front: A square, regular hexagon and another regular polygon meet at a point. How many sides does the other polygon have?

options.explanation: The square and hexagon contribute 90° and 120°, leaving 150°. Its exterior angle is 30°, so the regular polygon has 360° ÷ 30° = 12 sides.
A regular hexagon has interior angle 120°, not the required 150°. The missing angle is 360° - 90° - 120° = 150°, corresponding to 12 sides.
A regular octagon has interior angle 135°, so the three angles would total only 345°. The required interior angle is 150°, which belongs to a 12-sided polygon.
A regular decagon has interior angle 144°, making the total 354° rather than 360°. The missing 150° angle gives exterior angle 30° and therefore 12 sides.
